title: How Powerful is Graph Filtering for Recommendation

problem.claim: The paper examines the power and limitations of graph filtering for recommendation in graph convolutional network methods.

gap.claim: Existing graph-filtering approaches are limited by lack of generality and lack of expressive power.

contributions.claim: The paper identifies lack of generality as a limitation of graph filtering for recommendation.
The paper theoretically shows that effective linear GCNs for collaborative filtering cannot generate arbitrary embeddings.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that graph filters fail to denoise sparse data when noise is scattered across all frequencies.
The authors report that supervised training performs worse on dense data when noise is concentrated in middle frequencies removable by graph filters without training.
The authors report a theoretical result that optimal data representations may be unreachable by linear GCNs.

narrative_sequence.summary: GCN effectiveness for recommendation has been attributed to spectral graph filtering.
Most GCN-based methods use graph filtering, optionally followed by low-rank mapping, with supervised optimization.
The paper presents lack of generality as a limitation of graph filtering.
The paper presents lack of expressive power as a second limitation.
Linear GCNs effective for collaborative filtering cannot generate arbitrary embeddings, so optimal representations may be unreachable.

source_observation.claim: Graph-filtering effectiveness depends on the distribution of noise across frequencies and data sparsity or density.

interpretation.claim: A filtering method's usefulness may depend on whether its spectral assumptions match the data's noise structure.

application.claim: When designing recommendation models, assess noise distribution and data density before choosing graph filtering or supervised training.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this design consideration applies beyond the described recommendation setting.

unknowns: No datasets, metrics, baselines, or quantitative results are specified.
The abstract does not provide the proof details or characterize which embeddings are unreachable.
The abstract does not describe the proposed method, if any.
